stem:
Rudo farms in natural region II near Chinhoyi. She plans to grow 3 ha of maize. A soil test of the field gave these results.

| Test | Result |
| --- | --- |
| pH | 4.9 (strongly acid) |
| Phosphorus | Low |
| Potassium | Medium |
| Magnesium | Low |

She will apply Compound D (assume 7% N) at 375 kg/ha at planting and ammonium nitrate (assume 34.5% N) at 200 kg/ha as top dressing. Lime and fertiliser are sold in 50 kg bags.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the nutrient whose shortage would cause purple leaves on the young maize in this field.
parts.explanation: Phosphorus (low in the test, and locked up by acidity).

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name the type of lime Rudo should use, given the soil test.
parts.explanation: Dolomitic lime corrects acidity and supplies the low magnesium.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Lime is recommended at 3 t/ha. Calculate the number of bags of lime needed.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of bags of Compound D needed. Round UP to whole bags.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Calculate the total mass of nitrogen applied per hectare from both fertilisers, in kg, to two decimal places.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: When should the ammonium nitrate be applied?

options.content: In split doses to the growing crop, e.g. at knee height and again later
All of it mixed with the lime a month before planting
options.rationale: Lime with ammonium fertiliser loses ammonia; too early also leaches.

options.content: All of it placed in the planting hole together with the seed at planting
options.rationale: This would burn the seed and leach.

options.content: After harvest, to prepare for the next season
options.rationale: Too late to help this crop.

parts.explanation: Split top dressing matches nitrogen supply to rapid growth and reduces leaching.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Explain how liming the field with the lime you named in (b) will help Rudo get more value from her fertiliser.

points.description: Raising the pH releases phosphorus locked up by iron and aluminium / removes aluminium toxicity so roots grow well.
Healthier roots and active soil bacteria (nitrifiers) take up and use more of the applied nutrients, so less is wasted.
Dolomitic lime also supplies the magnesium (and calcium) that the soil test shows is low.

parts.explanation: Lime improves nutrient availability and uptake.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Describe and explain how Rudo should fertilise this maize crop, from preparing the land to tasselling.

points.description: Test the soil and lime with dolomitic lime well before planting (dry season), broadcast and worked in.
Reason: lime acts slowly; it raises pH and supplies magnesium.
Apply Compound D as a basal dressing at planting, banded or placed beside but not touching the seed.
Reason: P and K move little and are needed for early root growth; contact burns seed.
Add manure or compost where available to improve organic matter and nutrient holding.
Top dress ammonium nitrate in split doses on moist soil beside the plants (e.g. about knee height and before tasselling).
Reason: nitrogen leaches easily and is needed most during rapid vegetative growth; not on wet leaves (scorch).
Watch for deficiency signs (yellow V on old leaves for N, purpling for P) and adjust; keep weeds controlled so they do not take the fertiliser.

parts.explanation: A programme in order, with reasons: lime, basal, organic matter, split top dressing, monitoring.

explanation: Soil test interpretation, lime and fertiliser calculations, and a reasoned fertiliser programme for maize.
hints: For the long part, follow the season in order and give a reason for each step.

stem: Chipo grows tomatoes in the dry season on a 30 m × 30 m plot near Mutare, using drip irrigation from a borehole. The plot has 25 drip lines, each 30 m long, with an emitter every 30 cm. Each emitter delivers 2 L per hour.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the part of the drip system that removes sand and silt from the water.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the total number of emitters on the plot.
parts.explanation: 30 m = 3000 cm; 3000 ÷ 30 = 100 per line; × 25 lines = 2,500 emitters.
parts.workedSolution: 1. 30 m = 3000 cm; 3000 ÷ 30 = 100 per line; × 25 lines = 2,500 emitters.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the total flow of the system, in litres per hour.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: The crop needs 5 mm of water over the whole plot. Calculate how many minutes the system must run.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Why do tomatoes under drip irrigation usually suffer less from leaf diseases than tomatoes under sprinklers?

options.rationale: Correct: fungal spores need wet leaves.

options.content: The plants grow faster and outgrow every disease
options.rationale: Leaf wetness, not growth rate, is the key.

parts.explanation: Overhead watering wets the foliage, which favours fungal infection.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Explain why irregular watering can cause blossom-end rot in tomatoes.

points.description: Calcium reaches the fruit dissolved in water moving through the plant.
When the soil dries out between waterings, too little calcium reaches the fruit, so tissue at the blossom end collapses.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: State **two** routine maintenance tasks for Chipo's drip system.

points.description: Clean the filter regularly.
Flush the drip lines / check and repair leaks / replace blocked emitters.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Explain how drip irrigation, correctly managed, can improve the yield and quality of Chipo's tomato crop compared with furrow irrigation.

points.description: Drip delivers water to the root zone, so little is lost by evaporation, runoff and deep drainage; the limited borehole water irrigates more plants.
Frequent small applications keep soil moisture even, reducing stress, fruit cracking and blossom-end rot.
Leaves stay dry, so fewer fungal leaf diseases and sprays are not washed off.
Fertigation supplies nutrients directly to the roots in small, frequent doses, reducing leaching.
Fewer weeds grow between the rows because the soil there stays dry.
Fruit stays clean (no soil splash), improving marketable quality.
Management needed: filter and flush to prevent blocked emitters; schedule irrigation to crop stage and weather; avoid over-watering.
Comparison: furrow is cheaper but wastes water on sandy soils, wets the soil surface widely and gives less even moisture.
